title: BradEngine

contributors.contribution: Jamie built BradEngine partly as a platform for teaching his two sons programming. They used it together to build games, multiplayer demos, physics experiments, and other learning projects.

description:
BradEngine is a reusable JavaScript and HTML5 Canvas game/application engine I developed from 2019 through roughly 2022. It grew into a broad platform for games, custom 2D and 3D rendering, networking, physics, voxel terrain, ray casting, cellular automata, machine learning, and technical experimentation. Its modular lifecycle and reusable engine structure became an important architectural precursor to GameEngineTS.

View the source and demos on GitHub

sections.title: Reusable Engine Architecture
paragraphs: BradEngine was designed to minimize project-specific programming by moving common application and game responsibilities into reusable engine systems.
Projects were built from cooperating classes and shared engine services rather than one large procedural script.

sections.title: Level Lifecycle
paragraphs: Levels derived from a shared LevelInterface-style abstraction and implemented focused lifecycle responsibilities.

sections.title: Resource Management
paragraphs: BradEngine supported project resource discovery and shared media loading for images, sounds, fonts, meshes, and other assets.
Projects could use common shared media while keeping their own resources organized separately.

sections.title: Configurable Runtime
paragraphs: Each project could configure engine behavior from its own page, including display sizing, debugging, networking, frame rate, physics timing, and script loading.

sections.title: Canvas Rendering
paragraphs: HTML5 Canvas was the primary rendering surface.
The engine supported 2D drawing, UI, particles, software-rendered 3D, overlays, diagnostic displays, and offscreen rendering.

sections.title: Layered and Offscreen Rendering
paragraphs: Projects could combine independent visual systems in one frame, such as a 3D scene, particle field, HUD, radar, cockpit graphics, and diagnostic monitors.
Secondary Canvas buffers could be rendered independently and composited into the main display.

sections.title: Homemade 3D Rendering Pipeline
paragraphs: BradEngine included a native software 3D rendering pipeline.
The dedicated 3D portfolio card covers the renderer in greater depth.

sections.title: Voxel Terrain
paragraphs: BradEngine included voxel-world experiments with generated chunks and persistent terrain data.
Web Workers were used for voxel terrain generation so heavier generation work could run outside the main rendering thread.

sections.title: Ray Casting
paragraphs: The engine workspace included ray-casting experiments, including textured raycasting for early first-person rendering techniques.

sections.title: Particle Systems
paragraphs: BradEngine included reusable particle-system support used across visual and gameplay experiments.

sections.title: Physics and Collision
paragraphs: I built homemade 2D physics and collision experiments and also used established libraries when appropriate.

sections.title: Working Multiplayer Networking
paragraphs: BradEngine included working browser-to-browser multiplayer using WebRTC and PeerJS.
My sons and I successfully ran multiplayer technology demos together on separate machines.

sections.title: Networking as an Engine System
paragraphs: Networking was handled as reusable engine infrastructure rather than embedded independently into every project.
Projects could configure network behavior and update timing alongside rendering and physics timing.

sections.title: Artificial Neural Networks
paragraphs: BradEngine also became a platform for machine-learning exercises and neural-network experiments.

sections.title: Cellular Automata
paragraphs: The project included original JavaScript implementations of cellular-automata systems and interactive simulation experiments.

sections.title: Event-Driven and Arcade Projects
paragraphs: BradEngine supported a wide range of game and architecture experiments, including event-driven action games, arcade-style projects, drawing tools, simulations, and reusable gameplay systems.

sections.title: Example Project Ecosystem
paragraphs: The repository contains a broad collection of standalone examples and learning projects built on the shared engine.

sections.title: 3D Asteroids Architecture Example
paragraphs: The 3D Asteroids project demonstrates the engine's modular structure.

A MainLevel class assembles reusable systems such as GameController, SkyBox, Particles, OuterSpace, Cockpit, Computer, MiniMap, and Camera while the engine supplies common lifecycle, rendering, resource, input, and scene infrastructure.

sections.title: Teaching Through Real Systems
paragraphs: BradEngine was also used as a practical teaching environment for my sons.

Rather than hiding programming behind a simplified educational interface, they learned by working with real classes, engine lifecycles, graphics, multiplayer networking, physics, and application structure.

sections.title: Basic Reusable Application Designer
paragraphs: The name BradEngine came from my son's name and the backronym Basic Reusable Application Designer.
Although the name started playfully, the engine ultimately became broad enough that the description fit surprisingly well.

sections.title: Precursor to GameEngineTS
paragraphs: BradEngine became an important architectural ancestor of GameEngineTS.
Both emphasize reusable engine systems, explicit lifecycle responsibilities, modular project code, and reducing the amount of custom programming needed to assemble a game.
GameEngineTS later formalized and significantly expanded ideas that were already emerging in BradEngine.

historicalNotes: BradEngine development began in 2019 and continued for approximately three years.
BradEngine expands to Basic Reusable Application Designer and is also a reference to Jamie's son's name.
The platform was used for games, teaching projects, physics demos, networking demos, graphics experiments, machine-learning work, and simulation projects.
BradEngine used a shared src engine folder with examples, learning projects, common media, documentation, and reusable runtime code.
Its lifecycle included loadResources(), setup(), getKeyboardInput(), and update(delta).
The engine supported shared image, sound, font, mesh, and media loading.
The engine supported per-project configuration for display, debug, networking, rendering timing, and physics timing.
The homemade 3D renderer was native to BradEngine.
The 3D pipeline included meshes, cameras, lighting, terrain, height maps, morphing meshes, and voxel chunks.
Voxel terrain generation used Web Workers.
BradEngine included ray-casting and textured-raycasting experiments.
BradEngine included particle systems.
BradEngine included homemade 2D physics/collision work as well as Box2D, Cannon.js, and Three.js experiments.
BradEngine included cloth simulation experiments.
WebRTC / PeerJS multiplayer worked successfully between Jamie and his sons on separate machines.
BradEngine included artificial neural-network and machine-learning examples including XOR, graph/training, and Pong-related experiments.
BradEngine included cellular-automata implementations including Conway's Game of Life, elementary rule-number experiments, sand simulation, and interactive fire.
The repository includes a broad example ecosystem including 3D Asteroids, Space Boss, Voxel Engine, textured raycasting, cloth physics, Fire Finger, Solar System, Sand Sim, Starfield, and ANN XOR.
The architecture was modular and class-based but was not yet the fully formalized component-oriented architecture later used by GameEngineTS.
BradEngine is a direct architectural precursor to GameEngineTS.
